experiments.kernel: s += data[idx[i]] for i in 0..n-1; idx is the identity or a random permutation, so both variants add the same n values
sum of the values >= 128 among n bytes, written with an if (branchy) or with a bit mask (branchless), over the same bytes sorted or in random order
sum of n 20-bit values held in a primitive array, a container of boxed numbers, or objects with one field

hypotheses.statement: With 64 MB of data (more than the 24 MB L3 cache), gathering through a random permutation is at least 4x slower per element than through the identity.
hypotheses.why: Sequential indices touch each 64-byte cache line 16 times and the prefetcher streams it in; random indices miss L3 on almost every load and pay a DRAM round trip.

hypotheses.statement: With 16 KB of data (fits in the 48 KB L1 data cache), the random permutation costs at most 1.5x the identity.
hypotheses.why: When every line is already in L1 the access order no longer matters much.

hypotheses.statement: In V8 with Int32Array and 64 MB of data, the random permutation is at least 4x slower per element than the identity.
hypotheses.why: TurboFan compiles the typed-array gather to plain loads, so the hardware effect should match Java's.

hypotheses.statement: In V8 with 16 KB of data, the random permutation costs at most 1.5x the identity.
In CPython with 2M list elements (about 80 MB of pointers and int objects), the random permutation is at least 1.5x slower per element than the identity.
hypotheses.why: Each element is a pointer to a separate int object, so a random order misses cache twice per element; the interpreter's own cost per element (tens of ns) dilutes the ratio.

hypotheses.statement: In CPython with 4096 list elements, the random permutation costs at most 1.2x the identity.
hypotheses.why: All objects fit in L2, and interpreter overhead dominates.

hypotheses.statement: The branchy kernel is at least 3x slower on bytes in random order than on the same bytes sorted.
hypotheses.why: Random bytes make the >= 128 branch a coin flip, so the predictor misses about half the time (about 15 to 20 cycles each); sorted bytes switch the outcome once.

hypotheses.statement: The branchless (bit mask) kernel costs at most 1.2x more on random bytes than on sorted bytes.
hypotheses.why: Without a data-dependent branch there is nothing to mispredict.

hypotheses.statement: In V8 the branchy kernel is at least 3x slower on random bytes than on sorted bytes.
In V8 the branchless kernel costs at most 1.2x more on random bytes than on sorted bytes.
In CPython the branchy kernel is at least 1.2x slower on random bytes than on sorted bytes.
hypotheses.why: The interpreter's conditional jump follows the data, so it is mispredicted on random bytes, but each element also costs tens of ns of interpreter work.

hypotheses.statement: In CPython the branchless kernel costs at most 1.1x more on random bytes than on sorted bytes.
Summing an ArrayList<Integer> is at least 3x slower than summing an int[] with the same values.
hypotheses.why: The list holds 4-byte references to 16-byte Integer objects, so every element costs an extra dependent load, and the int[] loop can be vectorized.

hypotheses.statement: A boxed Long accumulator (Long sum += v) allocates at least 16 bytes per element.
hypotheses.why: Each += creates a new Long through Long.valueOf, and the value cache only covers -128 to 127.

hypotheses.statement: The boxed Long accumulator is at least 2x slower than a primitive long accumulator over the same int[].
hypotheses.why: One allocation per element plus the young-generation collections it causes.

hypotheses.statement: In V8, summing an array of {v} objects is at least 2x slower than summing an Int32Array with the same values.
hypotheses.why: Every element is a pointer to a heap object whose field must be loaded, instead of a contiguous 4-byte integer.

hypotheses.statement: In V8, a plain Array of small integers (PACKED_SMI_ELEMENTS) costs at most 1.5x an Int32Array.
hypotheses.why: Small integers are stored unboxed (tagged) inside the array, so there is no pointer chasing, only tag checks and wider elements.

hypotheses.statement: In CPython, summing an array('q') is no slower than summing a list of the same ints (textbook view: unboxed storage is faster).
hypotheses.why: array('q') stores 8-byte machine integers contiguously, while a list stores pointers to separate int objects.

hypotheses.statement: In CPython, summing one attribute of objects with __slots__ is at least 1.5x slower than summing a list of ints.
hypotheses.why: Each element adds an attribute lookup through the type's slot descriptor and one more dependent load.
